description:
Wesam Saad examines what can hinder prayer through a discussion of motives, faith and relationships. Reading Psalm 66:18 alongside James 4:3, he argues that a request may appear good while serving a selfish desire. He challenges listeners to examine their motives without imagining that God requires complete sinlessness before they may approach him. The distinction matters for believers who recognise their continuing struggle with sin.

James 1:5–7 leads into a sustained discussion of active faith during trials. Saad rejects the assumption that faith operates automatically simply because someone is a Christian. Believers must deliberately trust God and act on what they know of his character. He distinguishes the faith shared by believers in salvation from particular spiritual gifts, explaining that receiving faith from God does not remove the responsibility to exercise it.

The closing questions explore how unresolved anger, treatment of a spouse and unforgiveness relate to prayer. Saad resists a mechanical rule that every failing cancels every request, while warning that selfishness can shape both relationships and petitions. He encourages honest self-examination and repentance, leaving the positive conditions for answered prayer to the next study.

questions.question: Why does Saad reject reading Psalm 66:18 as a requirement of complete sinlessness before prayer?
questions.answer: He points out that believers continue to discover and fight sinful desires. A rule requiring perfect awareness and repentance in every area would prevent any honest believer from approaching God. He instead focuses on the relationship between a particular request and the motive behind it.

questions.question: How does James 4:3 inform his explanation of wrong motives?
questions.answer: Saad connects asking without receiving to asking in order to spend the answer on one’s pleasures. He uses this to examine the desire driving a request, rather than judging the request only by how religious or respectable its subject appears.

questions.question: How might a request for another person’s good still be selfish?
questions.answer: The discussion gives examples of seeking someone’s conversion to protect one’s reputation or make life easier, or seeking healing chiefly for personal convenience. Saad urges listeners to examine whether love and God’s purposes are driving the request or whether it serves self-interest.

questions.question: What does Saad mean by exercising faith actively during trials?
questions.answer: He means deliberately trusting God rather than assuming faith will function on autopilot. He urges believers to remind themselves of God’s truth and respond in obedience, instead of letting changing thoughts and circumstances continually unsettle their trust.

questions.question: Why does receiving faith as a gift not remove the need to exercise it?
questions.answer: Saad compares faith with repentance: receiving these from God does not mean believers stop actively trusting or repenting. He also distinguishes saving faith shared by Christians from particular gifts given for the church’s edification, avoiding the assumption that every use of the word “gift” means the same thing.

questions.question: Does being a believer mean that every request will receive the desired answer?
questions.answer: Saad explicitly rejects that conclusion. He is considering conditions that hinder prayer and says the positive conditions for answered prayer still need discussion. The session therefore does not promise that every sincere request will have the outcome the believer wants.

questions.question: How does the discussion connect treatment of a spouse with prayer?
questions.answer: In discussing 1 Peter 3, Saad argues that a person’s conduct and motives cannot be separated from praying for a spouse. Selfish or harsh treatment can contradict the desire being expressed in prayer and damage the relationship through which that person encounters the believer’s faith.

questions.question: What caution does Saad give about making a blanket rule from unresolved sin or unforgiveness?
questions.answer: He does not treat every unrelated failing as automatically cancelling every prayer, but urges examination of how selfish motives may carry across situations. He takes bitterness within the church seriously and also allows that asking God for patience and perseverance may be part of receiving help to overcome sin.
